title: Flicker's High Flight
markdown:
Buckle up, because I'm about to tell you about a place so wondrous, so unlike anywhere else, it makes my old maps look like scribbles! I’ve trekked through jungles humming with secret life and sailed seas that whisper ancient tales, but the Hanging Valleys? That’s a whole different marvel. The air there tastes of pine and the promise of distant snow, a crispness that wakes up your very bones. Imagine valleys that seem to float, stitched to the sky by misty veils, with streams that tumble down like liquid sunlight. And right there, nestled in a dwelling carved from a boulder the size of a sleepy bear, lived Tamsin-Gob.

She was a goblin with eyes like two bright, busy magpies, always spotting the next shiny thing or interesting puzzle. Her constant shadow was Pipkin, a ferret whose every twitch and tiny chirp was a language only Tamsin-Gob truly understood. Their days were usually a gentle hum of tinkering with mountain contraptions and sharing hearth-baked root bread. But the very heart of their little world, the sparkle in their days, was Flicker.

Flicker wasn't just any pet. He was a puffin, and what a puffin! His beak was a splash of sunset colours, and his spirit danced as free as the mountain winds. He loved a good waddle, a daring dive, and most of all, he loved to soar. His feathers, a sleek black and white, gleamed in the sun. His bright, curious eyes missed nothing, especially sunbeams, which he’d chase with joyful abandon, leaving small, delightful messes in his wake.

“Pipkin,” Tamsin-Gob said one sun-drenched morning, her voice a soft, flustered sound that was unusual for her. “Pipkin, have you seen Flicker? He’s not in his nest, and he’s not by the sun-dial!”

Pipkin, who had been polishing a tiny brass cog with a piece of moss, froze. His little nose twitched, sampling the air. He looked towards the open doorway, where the sunlight streamed in like a golden invitation, and then he looked up, his bright eyes wide with a sudden realization.

And there, against the vast, impossibly blue canvas of the sky, was Flicker. A small, dark speck, rising, rising, rising on invisible currents. He wasn't just flying; he was exploring. He was… gone. Higher and higher he spiraled, a tiny white flash against the deep azure.

A tremor shook Tamsin-Gob's shoulders. Her hands flew to her mouth. This was no lost slipper or misplaced tool. This was her Flicker, her mischievous, beloved Flicker, heading for the very roof of the world. A cold, sharp worry began to prickle at her heart. He was so small, and the sky so immense. “Oh, Flicker!” she whispered, a wobble in her voice.

Pipkin darted forward, a blur of brown fur. He nudged Tamsin-Gob’s hand with his soft nose, then chirped urgently, his body language a clear message: *We go. We get him. Don’t worry.* His confidence was a small, but powerful, anchor.

And so, they set out. Tamsin-Gob, her trusty walking staff in hand, followed Pipkin onto the winding mountain path. It was a dappled track where pine shadows lay striped across the ancient stone, the air growing cooler as they ascended. The wind, a constant companion in these altitudes, whispered secrets through the gnarled branches of fir trees that leaned as if in greeting, their needles rustling like tiny applause. Pipkin scampered ahead, his keen eyes scanning the way, his tail a vibrant question mark.

They rounded a bend that opened onto a breathtaking vista of the lower valleys, and there, perched precariously on a ledge that looked like it had been chipped from the sky itself, was Grumble-Snout. His mobile trading post, a sturdy, brightly painted cart pulled by a remarkably patient, shaggy mountain yak, overflowed with a bewildering assortment of items. He greeted them with a grin that showed off his surprisingly clean teeth, and a voice that had the gravelly warmth of a rumbling avalanche.

“Tamsin-Gob! Pipkin! A fine day for an expedition, wouldn't you say?” he boomed, tipping a cap adorned with a colourful feather. “Out for a bit of mountain exploration, are we?”

Tamsin-Gob, trying to keep her voice steady despite the tremor in her heart, explained her predicament. “Grumble-Snout, have you by any chance seen a puffin flying very, very high? Much higher than usual?”

Grumble-Snout stroked his chin, his eyes twinkling with a mixture of concern and opportunity. “A puffin, you say? High? Well, I might have just the thing!” He rummaged enthusiastically in his cart, his elbows bumping against various jars and trinkets. He produced a large, intricately woven net made of what looked like spun moonlight. “Behold!” he declared, unfurling it with a flourish. “The Sky-Fisher’s Delight! Perfect for snagging creatures from the ether, right out of the blue!”

Tamsin-Gob stared at the net. It was beautifully made, no doubt, but Flicker wasn't a fish. He was her pet, her feathered friend. “That’s… very kind, Grumble-Snout,” she said politely, her voice tinged with a hint of desperation. “But I don’t think Flicker is one for fishing, even from the sky.”

“Ah, right you are!” Grumble-Snout chuckled, tucking the net away with surprising speed. “A discerning creature, I’m sure. Perhaps something else then.” He rummaged again, this time producing a long, slender pole topped with a polished crystal. “The Cloud-Walker’s Staff! Guaranteed to keep your feet dry, even when traversing the fluffiest cumulus! You’ll never get a soggy sock again!”

Tamsin-Gob’s shoulders slumped. A walking stick for clouds was of absolutely no use when Flicker was miles above the nearest wisp of vapour, a tiny speck against the overwhelming blue. Just as despair began to settle in her chest like a heavy stone, a sound, faint but unmistakable, echoed down from the peaks. *Honk! Honk!*

It was Flicker!

“He’s up there!” Tamsin-Gob cried, pointing with a trembling finger towards the highest, most ancient-looking pine tree she had ever seen. It stood sentinel against the sky, its trunk as wide as a small house, its branches reaching like wizened fingers towards the heavens. And there, perched on its very topmost twig, a mere needle point against the vastness, was Flicker. He looked remarkably unconcerned, a tiny statue surveying the world spread out below him like a rumpled green and brown blanket.

They scrambled upwards, the pine shadows stretching and shrinking like playful spirits as the sun climbed higher. Tamsin-Gob called Flicker’s name, her voice carried away by the brisk mountain breeze. She cooed and whistled, mimicking his favourite playful sounds, offering imaginary treats. But Flicker, though he watched her, seemed utterly content in his lofty perch. He wasn't stuck, not truly. He was simply… enjoying the view. He tilted his head, his beak catching the sunlight, as if contemplating the sheer scale of it all.

Pipkin, ever observant, darted around the base of the great pine, his nose to the ground. He nudged a loose coil of something grey and springy with his paw. Tamsin-Gob recognized it instantly. It was a length of licorice rope, strong and sweet-smelling, that Grumble-Snout often sold for building goblin kites and making sturdy, chewable toys.

And then, a brilliant idea sparked in Tamsin-Gob’s mind, as bright and sudden as a lightning strike. Flicker loved soaring. He loved seeing the world from a new perspective. But he also loved her, and he loved treats. He wasn't trying to escape; he was trying to *see*.

Grumble-Snout, as if summoned by the very thought of a trade or a potential problem, reappeared, his yak patiently chewing its cud. “Trouble, Tamsin-Gob?” he asked, pulling a small, brass whistle from his pouch. “I’ve got just the thing! This will call any bird, guaranteed! It’s tuned to the frequency of… well, something bird-like, at any rate!”

Tamsin-Gob smiled, a genuine, warm smile that reached her bright, curious eyes. “Grumble-Snout,” she said, her voice clear and steady, carrying a new confidence. “I think I have just what Flicker needs. And I think I know how to get him down safely.”

She took the licorice rope. She didn't try to climb the impossibly tall tree. Instead, she looped the rope, creating a sturdy, wide cradle that swayed gently in the breeze. Then, she reached into her satchel and pulled out a truly magnificent, glistening mountain berry – plump, crimson, and bursting with sweet juice. It was one of Flicker’s absolute favourites. She dangled it just within reach of his beak, where it sparkled enticingly.

Flicker eyed the berry. He eyed the licorice rope-swing, which looked strangely like a new kind of perch. He eyed Tamsin-Gob, his familiar, loving goblin, who was offering him not just a treat, but a ride. He gave a happy *honk!* and, with a little hop, landed not on the ground, but squarely in the licorice cradle.

With Pipkin holding one end of the rope steady, his small body braced against a thick root, Tamsin-Gob gently, carefully, lowered Flicker. The licorice rope swayed just enough to feel like a thrilling descent, a controlled flight. The berry remained tantalizingly close, a reward for his bravery. The wind whistled a cheerful tune around them.

Back on the ground, Flicker waddled into Tamsin-Gob’s waiting arms, nuzzling her cheek with his beak, letting out a series of contented chirps. The adventure had been thrilling for him, a grand exploration of the skies. For Tamsin-Gob, it had been a lesson in understanding his curious spirit.

That evening, back in their cozy home, Tamsin-Gob built Flicker a new perch. It was higher than any branch in their garden, a specially crafted platform that allowed him to gaze at the sky, the distant peaks, and the swirling mists, just as he loved to do. But it was also safe, secure, and close to home, where his favourite goblin and ferret friends waited.

Flicker honked his happy approval, snuggled close to Tamsin-Gob, a contented puffin with a newfound appreciation for safe heights. Pipkin purred, a rumbling sound of pure contentment, curled up on Tamsin-Gob’s lap. And Tamsin-Gob knew, with a warmth that spread through her like the morning sun, that sometimes the greatest adventures are not about reaching the highest heights alone, but about finding a way to share them. And that, my friends, is a valuable thing to remember, whether you’re a goblin, a ferret, or a puffin with a love for the sky.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
